title: Kafka Producers: Acks, Batching, Idempotence & Retries
summary: A dense field guide to the Kafka producer path: how acks levels trade durability for latency, how batching and linger control throughput, how the idempotent producer kills duplicates, and how retries, ordering and error handling really behave in production.

chapters.title: The Producer Path: What Send Actually Does
points: KafkaProducer is thread-safe and expensive to create — share one instance per app, not one per request
producer.send(record) is asynchronous: it returns Future<RecordMetadata> immediately, it does not hit the broker
Five stages of a send: serialize -> partition -> accumulate into batch -> Sender thread groups by broker -> ProduceRequest over the wire
Two threads matter: the caller (application) thread does serialize+partition+append; the background Sender (I/O) thread does the network
RecordAccumulator holds a per-TopicPartition deque of batches in a memory pool of size buffer.memory (default 32 MB)
Serializers convert key and value to byte[]; broker never inspects the payload, it stores opaque bytes
Partitioner: explicit partition > key hash (murmur2 of key bytes % numPartitions) > sticky partitioner when key is null
Sticky partitioner (default since 2.4) fills one partition's batch, then switches — bigger batches, lower latency, still even long-run spread
RecordMetadata returned on success carries topic, partition, offset, timestamp — offset is the broker-assigned log position
Callback form: send(record, (metadata, exception) -> ...) — exactly one of the two args is non-null
Callbacks run on the Sender thread: never block or do slow work inside them or you stall all sends
send().get() makes it synchronous: correct, simple, and roughly 100x slower throughput — batching collapses to one record
Gotcha: a try/catch around send() only catches serialization and buffer-full errors, never broker-side failures
producer.flush() blocks until all buffered records complete; close() flushes then releases the connection

chapters.title: acks: The Durability Dial
points: acks controls how many replicas must acknowledge a write before the broker responds to the producer
acks=0: fire-and-forget. Producer never waits, offset returned is -1, records lost silently on broker failure or full socket buffer
acks=1: leader writes to its log and replies. Lost if leader dies before followers replicate that record
acks=all (== acks=-1): leader waits for all in-sync replicas to fetch the record; the durable choice
acks=all is the default since Kafka 3.0 (with enable.idempotence=true); older clients defaulted to acks=1
acks=all alone is NOT enough — pair with broker/topic min.insync.replicas or 'all ISR' can mean 'just the leader'
min.insync.replicas=2 with replication.factor=3 is the standard safe triple: tolerates one broker down, still rejects writes at two down
When ISR count < min.insync.replicas the broker rejects the produce with NotEnoughReplicasException — producer sees an error rather than silently losing data
acks=all does not wait for fsync to disk — it waits for the record to be in each replica's page cache; durability is replication, not flush
Latency cost: acks=0 ~fastest, acks=1 adds one leader write, acks=all adds a follower fetch round trip (typically single-digit ms in-DC)
Throughput cost of acks=all is far smaller than people assume because batching amortizes the wait across many records
Choice table: metrics/logs where loss is tolerable -> acks=1; payments, orders, CDC, event sourcing -> acks=all
acks=0 is incompatible with idempotence and transactions; the producer refuses to start with both configured
unclean.leader.election.enable=true silently defeats acks=all by letting an out-of-sync replica become leader — keep it false

chapters.title: Batching: batch.size and linger.ms
points: Kafka batches at the partition level: one batch = many records for one TopicPartition, compressed and CRC'd as a unit
batch.size (default 16384 bytes) is a byte cap, not a record count — a full batch is sent immediately regardless of linger
linger.ms (default 0) is how long the Sender waits for more records before sending a non-full batch
linger.ms=0 does NOT mean no batching: records that arrive while a previous request is in flight still coalesce
The two are a race: batch ships at whichever fires first — batch.size full OR linger.ms elapsed
Typical high-throughput tuning: batch.size=32768..131072 with linger.ms=5..100
Bigger batches raise throughput and compression ratio, and reduce broker request rate and CPU per record
Cost of batching is bounded added latency: worst-case producer-side delay ~= linger.ms
A record larger than batch.size gets its own oversized batch — batch.size is not a hard cap on record size
max.request.size (default 1 MB) caps one ProduceRequest; message.max.bytes on the broker must be >= it or writes are rejected
buffer.memory (default 32 MB) is the total accumulator pool; when exhausted, send() blocks up to max.block.ms (default 60s) then throws TimeoutException
compression.type: none | gzip | snappy | lz4 | zstd — applied per batch, so bigger batches compress much better
lz4/zstd are the usual picks: lz4 for CPU-cheap speed, zstd for the best ratio at moderate CPU
Broker stores the compressed batch as-is and consumers decompress — compression saves disk and network end to end
Gotcha: broker recompression happens if broker compression.type differs from the producer's, burning broker CPU — set it to 'producer'
Metrics to watch: batch-size-avg, records-per-request-avg, compression-rate-avg, record-queue-time-avg

chapters.title: Retries, Timeouts and In-Flight Requests
points: retries defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE in modern clients — retry count is no longer the real bound, time is
delivery.timeout.ms (default 120000) is the true upper bound on send(): covers batching time + all retries + all in-flight attempts
Invariant: delivery.timeout.ms >= linger.ms + request.timeout.ms; the producer refuses to start otherwise
request.timeout.ms (default 30000) bounds one attempt waiting for the broker's response before it is retried
retry.backoff.ms (default 100) waits between attempts; retry.backoff.max.ms (default 1000) caps exponential backoff with jitter
max.block.ms bounds send() and partitionsFor() blocking on metadata fetch or a full buffer — unrelated to delivery timeout
Retriable errors: NotLeaderOrFollowerException, LeaderNotAvailable, NetworkException, RequestTimedOut, NotEnoughReplicas
Non-retriable: RecordTooLargeException, SerializationException, AuthorizationException, InvalidTopicException — retrying can never help
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection (default 5) is how many unacked ProduceRequests can be outstanding per broker
Ordering hazard: without idempotence, max.in.flight > 1 + retries can reorder — batch 2 succeeds while retried batch 1 lands later
Pre-idempotence fix was max.in.flight=1, which crushed throughput; idempotence gives ordering back up to 5 in flight
A retry after a broker-side success but a lost ack produces a duplicate — this is the core at-least-once problem
On delivery timeout the callback receives TimeoutException and the outcome is genuinely unknown: may have been written
Retry storms are real: an under-replicated cluster plus MAX_VALUE retries can hold buffer.memory hostage and block producers

chapters.title: Idempotent Producer: Exactly-Once Per Partition
points: enable.idempotence=true makes broker-side retries produce no duplicates — on by default since Kafka 3.0
Producer obtains a Producer ID (PID) from the transaction coordinator via an InitProducerId request at startup
Every batch carries (PID, epoch, base sequence number); sequence numbers increment per partition, per producer
Broker keeps the last 5 sequence numbers per PID per partition in memory and in the log's producer state snapshot
Duplicate detection: an incoming batch whose sequence was already committed is acknowledged again but not appended
The broker returns the original offset for a deduped batch, so the producer's callback still sees a valid RecordMetadata
Ordering guarantee: the broker rejects out-of-order sequences with OutOfOrderSequenceException, so retries cannot reorder writes
This is why max.in.flight up to 5 is safe with idempotence — the broker enforces sequence order, not the client
Required config combination, auto-enforced: acks=all, retries>0, max.in.flight<=5 — a conflicting explicit value throws ConfigException
Cost is near zero: a few extra bytes per batch header plus a small broker-side map; leave it on
Scope limits: guarantees hold per partition, per producer session — a new producer instance gets a new PID and loses the dedupe history
Epoch bumps fence a zombie producer: the older epoch's writes get rejected with a fencing error
producer state expires after transactional.id.expiration.ms / when segments age out; a very idle producer can lose its state and see UNKNOWN_PRODUCER_ID
Idempotence is not end-to-end exactly-once: application-level double-send (retry above the client) still creates duplicates

chapters.title: Transactions: Atomic Multi-Partition Writes
points: Transactions extend idempotence from one partition to an atomic set of writes across partitions and topics
Set transactional.id to a stable, unique per-instance string — it is what survives restarts and enables fencing
API sequence: initTransactions() once, then beginTransaction() / send()... / commitTransaction() or abortTransaction()
initTransactions() fences any prior producer with the same transactional.id by bumping the epoch and aborting its open transaction
The transaction coordinator writes markers (commit/abort control records) into every partition the transaction touched
Consumers set isolation.level=read_committed to skip aborted records and stop at the Last Stable Offset (LSO)
isolation.level=read_uncommitted (default) shows aborted records — reading transactional output requires opting in
sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, groupMetadata) makes consume-process-produce atomic: the offset commit joins the transaction
This is exactly the mechanism Kafka Streams uses under processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2
transaction.timeout.ms (default 60s) must be <= broker transaction.max.timeout.ms (default 15 min) or initTransactions fails
Throughput cost is real: commit is a two-phase write of markers; batch many records per transaction, don't commit per record
ProducerFencedException, OutOfOrderSequenceException and authorization errors are fatal — close the producer, do not retry
KafkaException on commit is ambiguous only for retriable causes; abortTransaction() is the safe response to most failures
Transactions cost extra end-to-end latency for read_committed consumers: they cannot see records until the marker lands

chapters.title: Delivery Semantics End to End
points: At-most-once: acks=0 or retries=0 — never duplicates, can lose records; suitable for high-volume metrics
At-least-once: acks=all + retries — never loses, can duplicate; the pre-0.11 default and still the pragmatic norm
Exactly-once (within Kafka): idempotent producer for one partition, transactions across partitions, read_committed consumers
Comparison row — acks=0: latency lowest, durability none, duplicates none, loss likely under failure
Comparison row — acks=1: latency low, durability leader-only, duplicates possible on retry, loss on leader failover
Comparison row — acks=all + idempotence: latency slightly higher, durability ISR-wide, duplicates none, loss only on total ISR loss
Kafka's exactly-once is exactly-once processing inside Kafka, not exactly-once delivery to an external system
Writing to an external DB still needs idempotent upserts, a dedupe key, or the transactional outbox pattern
Consumer-side offset commit timing decides semantics too: commit before processing = at-most-once, commit after = at-least-once
Idempotent consumer design: dedupe on a business key or on (topic, partition, offset) stored with the write
A duplicate is only harmful if the downstream effect is not idempotent — 'set balance to X' is safe, 'add X' is not
Ordering guarantee is per partition only — global ordering needs a single partition and gives up parallelism
Keyed records preserve per-entity order: same key -> same partition -> ordered, which is what most systems actually need
Repartitioning (adding partitions) breaks key-to-partition stability and therefore breaks historical ordering per key

chapters.title: Error Handling and Common Mistakes
points: Mistake: ignoring the send() return value entirely — failures vanish and the app reports success it never got
Mistake: try/catch around send() and assuming it caught broker errors — it only sees synchronous serialize/buffer errors
Mistake: send().get() in a loop for 'safety' — turns a 100k msg/s producer into ~1k msg/s with zero durability gain
Mistake: heavy work inside the callback — the Sender thread is blocked and every partition's throughput drops
Mistake: creating a producer per request — connection churn, metadata refetch, and no batching at all
Mistake: forgetting close() — buffered records in the accumulator are simply lost on shutdown
Use close(Duration) in a shutdown hook so in-flight sends drain with a bound instead of hanging forever
Mistake: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1, which quietly degrades to leader-only durability
Mistake: leaving unclean.leader.election.enable=true, which can truncate acknowledged records
Mistake: setting retries=0 to 'avoid duplicates' when idempotence already solves duplicates without losing records
Mistake: huge linger.ms on a latency-sensitive path — added delay is invisible in throughput tests and painful in production
TimeoutException after delivery.timeout.ms means unknown outcome: log with the key, and let a downstream dedupe absorb the replay
RecordTooLargeException means fix max.request.size and broker message.max.bytes together, or shrink the payload
Fatal-vs-retriable: build the error branch on the exception type, not on a blanket retry-everything wrapper
Producing to a non-existent topic with auto.create.topics.enable=true silently creates a wrongly-configured topic

chapters.title: Tuning, Monitoring and Real Config Recipes
points: Throughput recipe: acks=1 or all, linger.ms=20..100, batch.size=131072, compression.type=lz4, buffer.memory=64MB+
Low-latency recipe: linger.ms=0, batch.size default, compression.type=none or lz4, max.in.flight=5
Max-durability recipe: acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, delivery.timeout.ms high, min.insync.replicas=2, RF=3, unclean election off
Key JMX metrics: record-send-rate, request-latency-avg, record-error-rate, record-retry-rate, batch-size-avg, buffer-available-bytes
record-queue-time-avg rising means the accumulator is backing up — the broker or network is the bottleneck, not the app
buffer-available-bytes trending to zero predicts send() blocking on max.block.ms before it happens
Diagnostic: high request-latency-avg with normal record-send-rate points at broker or ISR problems, not producer config
Rule of thumb: tune batch.size first, linger.ms second, compression third — most wins come from bigger batches
Compression benchmark ranking (typical JSON): zstd best ratio, gzip good ratio at high CPU, lz4 fastest, snappy in between
Scaling out: more producer instances help only if partition count allows — throughput ceiling is partitions x per-partition rate
Partition count sets the parallelism ceiling; too many partitions raises broker memory and end-to-end latency
max.block.ms is the config that turns a broker outage into either backpressure or a fast failure — pick deliberately
Test durability with real chaos: kill the leader mid-load and count records, don't trust config review alone
Producer interceptors (interceptor.classes) let you add tracing or auditing without touching call sites

chapters.title: Summary: The Producer Cheat Sheet
points: One-line mental model: send() buffers, the Sender batches, acks decides who must confirm, sequences kill duplicates
acks=0 loses, acks=1 loses on failover, acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 is the durable baseline
delivery.timeout.ms is the only bound that matters for how long a send can take — retries is effectively infinite
enable.idempotence=true is free correctness: no duplicates, no reordering, up to 5 in-flight requests
Transactions add atomicity across partitions and the consume-process-produce loop; they cost latency, not correctness
Ordering is per partition; keys pin entities to partitions; adding partitions breaks that pinning
Bigger batches almost always win: throughput, compression ratio, and broker CPU all improve together
linger.ms is the only knob that deliberately trades latency for throughput — everything else is a durability trade
Always handle the callback or the future; a fire-and-forget send is a silent data-loss policy
Always close the producer with a timeout on shutdown, or buffered records disappear
Kafka exactly-once ends at Kafka's boundary — external sinks still need idempotent writes or an outbox
Config invariants to memorize: delivery.timeout >= linger + request.timeout; max.request.size <= broker message.max.bytes; RF > min.insync.replicas
Default-good starting point for most services: acks=all, idempotence on, linger.ms=10, batch.size=65536, compression lz4
Debug order when producing is slow: check record-queue-time, then request-latency, then ISR health, then config
